Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) asked for certain information with regard to certain operations of the wheat board in connection with the supplying of seed wheat to the province of Saskatchewan. He made reference then to a car of wheat which had been delivered to a place called Coleville. I have a telegram with regard to that matter which I should like to read to the house. It is as follows:
Referring telephone conversation and reference to Coleville car. This small car of wheat ordered shipped to Coleville by Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture May ninth. Shipment was made May eleventh. We were advised by department this car had been ordered by a rural municipality in error and were instructed night of May twentieth to rebill to Lakehead. Instructions given railway morning May twenty-first and situation immediately dealt with. Accordingly this car arrived at Fort William May thirty-first.
My right hon. friend stated that according to the weekly statement by the wheat board there were apparently some two million bushels of seed wheat still left in the hands of the government.

speechtext: Of wheat; I did not say "seed wheat".

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, June 6, consideration in committee of Bill No. 31,

Transport Commission
to establish a board of transport commissioners for Canada, with authority in respect of transport by railways, ships and aircraft- Mr. Howe-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 35, subsection 1-Charges by agreement between parties.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Section 35, which introduces part V of the bill, contains a distinct departure in the matter of transportation control. I am not going to argue the matter at length because the bill was discussed thoroughly in the committee on railways and canals. However, when the bill was under consideration in the committee I made it clear that I was opposed to this part and particularly to these four sections, and indicated that I would oppose them when they came before the committee of the whole. I should like to state briefly the reasons for my objection to this part and to this particular section.
This section is a distinctly retrograde move. The board of railway commissioners was set up in 1904. For years previously chaos and discrimination and unfairness had existed in the railway transport business, both in Canada and in the United States. It will be recalled that powerful corporations in those earlier days would frequently secure privileges and advantages from the railway companies which were not open to smaller shippers or sometimes to other large shippers who were in a competitive position. These abuses were done away with in the United States by the appointment of the interstate commerce commission and the application of its code of laws, and in Canada by the appointment of the board of railway commissioners and the enactment of the Railway Act, with the various amendments that have been made since 1904.
I do not hesitate to pay tribute to the boards of railway commissioners that have been sitting in this country for the last thirty or so years. Almost always they have been presided over by able and distinguished men, sometimes by very distinguished men. Because of their findings a sort of case law has been built up which I believe is accepted. Their rulings are now recognized, generally speaking, as equitable and fair. The public interest has been well protected. It has been argued in support of this measure, which will set up a board of transport commissioners, that they will administer the law in the same manner as it has been administered in the past. I have no doubt they will, but the point is that by this part the board is instructed to permit agreements to be made 51952-229
between the railway companies and individual shippers.
Something that has been prohibited for years, something that has been recognized on no occasion, is now to become law: a private shipper and a railway company may enter into an agreement. I am quite aware it will be argued that this provision has been surrounded with the necessary safeguards, but the principle involved is a serious one. Under the Railway Act through the years unjust and unfair discrimination has been defined and its application guarded against. Furthermore, any discriminatory, competitive or special rate has been open to all shippers along the lines affected by the rate. Under this bill an agreement may be made with an individual shipper, and then provision is made to permit those who object to come before the board to State their case. If they can make good their case, there is no doubt in my mind that the board will do justice, but this is a reversal of the principle that has obtained in. the past.
Furthermore, this part limits the application of this provision to those who are defined in the bill as carriers. A carrier is defined as follows:
"Carrier" means any person engaged in the transport of goods or passengers for hire or reward to whom this act applies, and shall include any company which is subject to the Railway Act.
This bill does not apply to highway transport. I think it is quite clear that the intention of part, V is to give the railway companies a weapon which will enable them to compete with the trucks on the highways. The trucking companies are not to have access to this court in order to present any grievance they may have, nor will private individuals who are not carriers under this definition be allowed to appear. My submission before the committee was that the word "carrier" should be changed to "persons," that any person in Canada should be allowed to appear before the board in the same manner as he is permitted to appear before any court for the purpose of securing redress of grievances. As I have Stated already, under this bill a carrier is limited to those licensed under this legislation. This makes a definite distinction and limitation and is another reason why I am opposed to this part.
My main objection is that this bill introduces into our legislative control of railways the principle of granting permission to a railway company to make an agreement with a special shipper. Whether or not the agreement is unfair is to be decided after the agreement is made. If one will study the

Transport Commission

section carefully he will find that these are the words which control the possibility of a complainant making good his case:
Being the same goods as or similar goods to and being offered for carriage under substantially similar circumstances and conditions as the goods to which the agreed charge relates.
I submit it will be extremely difficult for a small shipper ever to demonstrate that he is prepared, although in competition with the big shipper, to ship goods under substantially similar circumstances and conditions as would the large shipper. For example, a large shipper may have outlets all over Canada. He makes an agreement with the railway company to carry all his freight, because that is the suggested excuse for this measure, that the railway can bargain to get all this shipper's freight and thus get away from their highway competitors some of the traffic the railways are now losing. So the shipper engages to ship all his freight over this line, and he gets in return a flat rate over different zones. Then the smaller shipper comes along. He perhaps serves only one section of the country. He is in direct competition with the large shipper so far as his goods are concerned, but he cannot show the same circumstances and conditions. The answer that will be made to him is obvious: You ship only a small quantity and operate only in a certain territory, while the large shipper ships all over Canada; therefore as the circumstances are not alike and the conditions are not similar you have no case. Yet, Mr. Chairman, the competition is there, and the small shipper will thus be more or less ruthlessly driven out of the market.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Was it not made clear that
the volume of traffic could not enter into the picture?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
But that is not a question of volume; it is a question of distribution. Let me put another case. In eastern Canada there is a large factory manufacturing a certain class of goods and distributing them right across western Canada, or as far west as they can go. There is a small factory on the Pacific coast, in an entirely different section, shipping freight east into the prairie markets. Now this small shipper would have to show that he was handling his business under the same conditions and circumstances as the large shipper in eastern Canada. But there is no parallel at all. His territory is different; the direction of the movement of his goods is different, the rate is different. The man in the east gets a low rate, and thus gets a very definite advantage in the movement of his goods westward. The conditions might be reversed. But the point I am making is that it will be almost an impossibility to show sub-

stantially similar circumstances and conditions to obtain in connection with the distribution of goods.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: These words are already in the Railway Act.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: The rate structure is predicated on similar circumstances and conditions, under the Railway Act.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Yes, but when a rate is fixed under the Railway Act anybody who ships any quantity, large or small, over that route gets exactly the same rate. The tariff is there and it is open to everybody and at all times, but in this case it is not.
I will give another instance, where I think unfair discrimination might arise in the operation of this act. Suppose there are two different types of goods, each of which is interchangeable and in competition with the other. I have no particular commodity in mind, but there are many lines of goods for which an entirely different line may be used in substitution according to the desire or prejudice of the customer. One line of goods might get a special rate. The competing goods could not because they are not the same class of goods, but a different type of goods, although the two lines of goods are in competition. And so I might go on down the line, giving many illustrations of the grave danger in giving this power or right. The main answer that was given in the committee to arguments of this kind was that the board of transport would be a fair and just board and could be trusted to guard against any abuses being allowed to develop. I frankly admit that I believe in the board of transport, the board of railway commissioners as it now is. I believe it will be fair. I am not complaining about the board of transport. I am complaining about the law that will govern the board of transport as this law will. This law not only authorizes but instructs them to sanction or approve of agreements, and they have no option in the matter.
I am not going to labour the question further. I am going to move a clause in amendment to the whole section; and if, Mr. Chairman, I am in order, I can do it now, or if necessary I can wait until the end of the section is reached. Perhaps I had better move it now so it will be in the minds of the members of the committee when they are considering the section. I move to amend section 35 by the addition of this clause after subsection 10:
Notwithstanding anything aforesaid the provisions of this bill shall not apply with respect to the carriage of goods between points or

Transport Commission
places in Canada where such carriage is only performed by carriers subject to the authority of the board of transport commissioners, and the board of transport commissioners shall not approve any agreement submitted to them which includes such carriage in the agreement or as a condition attached thereto.
Briefly the explanation is this. If this part of the bill is required by the railways to enable them to compete with highway competition, then it should limit in its operation to places where that competition exists; and if that competition does not exist, the agreed charges should not apply. My amendment would limit it in that way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out to the hon, member for Kootenay East that subsection 10 was carried yesterday.
Well, it can go after subsection 13.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Subsection 13 was
carried yesterday.
It can go in after subsection 1, as far as that is concerned.
It is just as appropriate there as anywhere, I think.

I think I can summarize my hon. friend's argument under three headings. In the first place he urges that " similar circumstances and conditions" means that in some cases certain competitive shippers might find themselves embarrassed because goods might be different and the lines or directions of traffic might be different. Competitive shipping, competition between shippers, does not exist with respect to different types of goods. Under the Railway Act, the rate structure is predicated upon similarity of circumstances and conditions. There is no departure from that principle in this bill. The words used prohibit unfair or unjust discrimination when traffic is moving under similar circumstances and conditions. This is the very principle of the Railway Act. To be able to allege unjust or unfair discrimination you must show that traffic of a similar nature, moving in a similar direction, under similar circumstances and conditions, is being charged at an unfair rate. In this act, if different goods are moving in different directions, under different circumstances and conditions, namely by highway, how could unjust or unfair discrimination be alleged?
My hon. friend further alleges that " agreed charges," referred to in section 35, are a departure from the underlying principles of the Railway Act. I submit that that is not so. Under the Railway Act there are three different types of rates:
. 51952-229J
1.	Standard mileage rates, which must be approved by the board. These rates are maximum rates. They cannot be exceeded; they must be submitted, approved and published. The board, after hearing, determines the maximum mileage rates permissible.
2.	Special tariffs, applicable to lumber, grain or other commodities moving in large volume, in trainload lots, carload lots, with respect to which there are special loading or unloading conditions or ceritain market conditions which permit, the particular commodity to be treated in a class by itself.
3.	Competitive rates, which in their managerial discretion carriers may publish to retain traffic which would otherwise go to rail or water competitors. Competitive rates need not be approved by the board. They are under the level prescribed by the standard mileage rates, and they can be published, and put into effect unless complained of.

All shippers are upon an
absolutely equitable basis.

Exactly. Any shipper who contends that he is injuriously affected' by competitive rates may make application to the board to object to their becoming effective, or for a revision or repeal of objectionable competitive rates.
In the exercise of its regulative power, the board never prevented a competitive rate from becoming effective without good reason. Competitive rates are permissible to enable rail carriers to retain traffic. In this act agreed rates are permitted to enable railway carriers to retain traffic which otherwise would go to their highway or water competitors.
They are under provincial regulation.
Not as to rates.
Not in Quebec.
I believe it is not so in almost all provinces.
They are regulated with respect to everything but rates, and may be regulated with respect to rates.

In England they are regulated. Highway carriers must take out a licence to carry on their trade. In Canada they are not regulated in that respect. In England they are regulated with respect to vehicles; the vehicle must come up to special standards and is subject to periodical inspection. Furthermore, drivers must submit to periodical physical examinations. These are important regulations: licences to cany on, standard
Transport Commission

modes of conveyances, drivers physically and periodically examined and licensed. We have nothing of this kind in Canada.
Highway raltes in England are governed by a rates tribunal; they come under the provisions of the transport act. We have no similar constitutional power in Canada.
They regulate the weight of the machine that may cross certain bridges.

That is with respect to road regulations. Departments controlling highways publish regulations to that effect. I do not believe they can be called as effective regulations between competitive carriers, as those proposed in this bill. Under the Railway Act, when competitive conditions exist between two points, between rail and water carriers, the rail carrier can publish competitive rates to retain traffic to his rails.
That is under the Railway Act.
Under the Railway Act. This bill does not contain anything else. We allow rail carriers to publish rates likely to retain the traffic to their own rails.
That is scarcely right. They do not publish a rate. We allow them to make a private agreement with an individual shipper, and that is vastly different from publishing a rate.
I hope to foe able to prove to my hon. friend that there is no difference at all. The agreed rate is a competitive rate.
Oh, no.
I will at least attempt to prove it.
The latter words of subsection 1 of section 35 disprove what the hon. member says.

No, I do not think so. Suppose a rate between points A and B, a rate of SI per hundred pounds. If the rail carrier published a rate of 90 cents per hundred pounds, with a view to retaining traffic to its rails, the highway carrier would immediately publish a rate of 85 cents per hundred pounds. The rail carrier would then have to publish a rate of 80 cents to outbid him.
Under this they do not publish it at all.

Let us not play upon words; if my hon. friend does not like the word "publish," let us say: "put into effect" a rate of 80 cents. This means a rate war, between the highway and the railway carriers. By agreed rates the rail carrier can go to a

shipper and say to him, "If you will give me all your traffic, for such a period, I will give you such a rate." This is the proposed agreed rate. An agreement is entered into. It is a contract. No rate war is possible. If they agree, the shipper and the carrier are bound. Competitive rates are suicidal for both the highway and the rail carriers.
It therefore seems that there is no difference in principle between the Railway Act and this proposed legislation, because the Railway Ac* enables the rail carrier to publish competitive rates to retain its traffic; herein, to avoid a rate war, we propose to allow the rail carrier to enter into such agreements with the shipper as will oblige the latter to route his traffic by a particular rail route, without a cut-throat rate reduction. There is therefore no fundamental difference in the principle of competitive rates under the Railway Act and the principle underlying these agreed rates.
My hon. friend's third point was that it is improper to refuse the highway carrier the privilege of appearing before the board to complain against agreed rates. May I suggest that the highway carrier is not unjustly discriminated against. The highway carrier is not regulated. He cannot be compelled to come to the board. His rates are not submitted for approval. He therefore competes with the rail and water carrier without control or regulation. He enters into agreements with shippers, and the rail or water carriers have no say in the matter and no remedy.
I submit that the rail carrier should be given the right to enter into an agreement with his own shippers, without the interference of the highway carrier. If the highway carrier can establish an agreed rate in favour of a shipper, why should not the rail or water carrier be granted the same privilege? My submission is therefore that there is no departure from the underlying principles of the Railway Act. The only principle herein involved is that we allow carriers to come to an agreement with shippers so as to retain traffic which otherwise would go to uncontrolled and unregulated highway carriers.

I should like to refer a
little further to what the hon. member (Mr. Vien) has just said about excluding the carrier from the right to appeal to the board. A shipper cannot appeal to the board unless that shipper has been shipping his goods by a carrier under the terms of this act. Take a shipper who is ten miles away from a railway terminal, and uses highway transport which competes with the railway. If an agreed charge is made with another shipper he would

Transport Commission
have no standing before the board, because the provision reads:
(6) Any shipper who considers that his business will be unjustly discriminated against if an agreed charge is approved and is made by the carrier, or that his business has been unjustly discriminated against as a result of the making of an agreed charge, may at any time apply to the board . . .
The general assumption is that that means any shipper. But turn to the definition of "shipper" and you find this:
"Shipper" means a person sending or receiving or desiring to send or receive goods by means of any carrier to whom this act applies.
That does not apply to a shipper who is not dealing with a earner under this act. My point is that any citizen of Canada has a right to appear before any court in Canada, a court of law or a court of equity. That is one of the fundamental rights of a citizen. I cannot sanction a law which will in effect rule a man or a company out from appearing before the courts. Under this we simply blackball those engaged in the highway traffic business.
And we are not free from biame in this. This parliament has never occupied the field that it might have occupied in controlling interprovincial and international transport by motor truck. That is admittedly our field; why does not the Minister of Transport occupy it as far as he can? Recognizing that we cannot interfere with the provincial jurisdiction, let this parliament occupy that field as far as it can, and then give to the trucking system its inherent common law right, that of appearing before a court to argue its case. I object to the idea that a court can be set up in this country to which a citizen is denied access.

A shipper and a highway
carrier can establish	an agreed	rate.	The
rail carrier or any competitive shipper cannot challenge such a rate. Why should the highway carrier, or a shipper using the highway have the right to challenge an agreement between a rail carrier and a shipper using the rails?

The	answer is	verysimple. In the one	ease	there	is no lawwhich applies to the trucking system. If there is a law applying to the trucking system he can apply. The	rail	carrier	and	other
forms of transport are covered by law, and it is the privilege of any person to appear before a court in this country and argue his case.

But how can they claim the
right to discuss a rail rate without allowing others the right to discuss their own rates?

That is simply because
we have not found the machinery to control the trucks.
We have no jurisdiction over highway traffic.
Yes, we have jurisdiction to control interprovincial traffic.

This section was discussed quite extensively at the last sitting, and I have no desire, and I think hon. members would not wish me, to traverse the ground we covered yesterday. However I think something should be said about the point of restricting access to the board of transport commissioners in the matter of agreed charges. Any person can appear before the board of transport commissioners in the matter of agreed charges who is allowed to appear before any court in the land; in other words, he must show an interest in the matter being discussed. He is allowed to appear if he is a shipper or a prospective shipper, that is if he wishes to ship goods. He is allowed to appear if he receives goods by the carrier, or if he wishes to receive goods-is a prospective receiver of goods. He is allowed to appear if he is a carrier under the act. What other classes of persons than these could possibly have an interest in a matter affecting rates? I cannot imagine any other class of person who could come before the board and show an interest.
Then as to discrimination. A rate is applied after exhaustive hearings by the board. Anyone affected by the rate has two options. One is that he can have exactly the same contract if he is shipping under substantially the same circumstances; and I think the act makes it perfectly clear that the size of the shipment does not enter into the situation as far as the similarity of the service is concerned. That is safeguarded in several clauses. Then if the shipper is not in a position to take advantage of the contract, but believes the contract will injuriously affect his business, he is given opportunity to appear before the board and object to the contract on the ground that if made it will injuriously affect his business. When we consider all the latitude that the transport board will have, when we consider the composition of the board, which after all is, as the railway board is and has been, a board for the protection of the public, I can hardly imagine that these agreed charges can be used in a manner injurious to the public at large.
As to the amendment offered by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) it would of course be restrictive to a point
Transport Commission

which would make the operation of agreed charges practically worthless. Cutting away all the verbiage, it would be necessary before an agreed charge could take effect to show that the particular traffic is subject to truck competition. The amendment says " must be subject to competition other than by a carrier under the act." Bulk water carriers would hardly meet that requirement, since bulk carriers do not carry the class of goods which is regulated under the act. So it comes down to this, that the amendment would have the effect of prohibiting the making of agreed charges except for a particular route which is subject to truck competition. One sees at once that that would prevent the sending of goods from the eastern part of Canada to the west under agreed charges, for the reason that there are no highways through part of northern Ontario; therefore goods originating in the east could not move under agreed charges farther than central Ontario. Every movement of goods under agreed charges would have to be subject to the test as to whether truck competition could be proven. I suggest that the amendment offered by the hon. member for Kootenay East is a method of rendering this part ineffective, and I must oppose it.

Mr. Chairman, two days ago I pointed out what I conceive to be the dangers in the adoption of the principle of agreed charges, under the terms provided for by the bill as it now stands. I pointed out that the basis of the present law is equality as to tolls and facilities. I find that that is the heading of the section in the Railway Act -Equality as to Tolls and Facilities. The first subsection is headed "equal tolls to be charged"; the second, "no discrimination"; the third, "carload quantities"; the fourth, "localities"; the fifth, "duty of the board"; and the sixth, "competitive points". The sixth subsection reads:
The board may declare that any places are competitive points within the meaning of this act.
Further it is pointed out in the Railway Act that no agreement can be made by which a railway company may give preference to any community or shipper. Certain well-defined classes of freight rates are also provided by the statute. As a matter of fact there are four: the standard tariff, the special tariff, the competitive tariff, and the joint tariff; with the addition of a special one which deals with exceptional circumstances such as bad crops and matters of that sort.
Then follows a provision with respect to how the tariffs come into operation, which I

do not intend to discuss. The competitive tariff, as mentioned by the hon. member for Outremont, came into being for many reasons, principally, on this continent, because of water carriage.
Now, whatever may be said as to the justice or injustice of the law, or the desirability or undesirability of our Railway Act, I think everyone will agree that as a result of what took place in the United States prior to the passing of the Interstate Commerce Act, and in Canada prior to the inquiries that were set up by the late Mr. Blair, which resulted in the passing of the Railway Act, equal tolls were not charged to all persons, and preferences were given to individuals-sometimes because of the volume of the traffic, and sometimes for other reasons The difficulty that arose in the United States caused a great deal of friction, and, as I say. resulted in the statute to which I referred. The result of the statute in Canada was just what I read a moment ago as the heading of the section, namely, equality as to tolls and facilities. As I pointed out, tolls are covered by four different kinds of tariffs, in addition to the very special class which deals with exceptional circumstances which need not be mentioned here, and which has .not been regarded by text writers as an additional classification.
We are to do away with that. We are to do away with the equality under the law which was tthe basis of our freight rate structure. The abuses which took place prior to the enactment of our Railway Act and the passage of the interstate commerce measure in the United States-all these are again to be possible, because there is no longer equality under 'the law with respect to freight rates. The minister says, or may say-and I judge from what he said the other day that he does say it-that it is no longer desirable to maintain that principle of equality under the law, and that agreed charges or charges that are agreed in contract rather than by parliamentary control shall prevail. An agreed charge is in essence a contractual charge. The present tariff toll is a statutory parliamentary charge, and until such time as under the existing law tolls are approved by the board they cannot recover a single cent. The law itself in terms declares that they cannot recover anything at all until such time as the tolls, whether they be one of the four classes I mentioned, any one of them, have been approved by the board.
I think my right hon. friend is wrong.

Yes.

Transport Commission

That applies equally to the
standard tariff.
No.
The special rates and competitive rates enter into effect without the approval of the board.

There is hardly a rate in
practical effect that is specifically approved by the board.

They have to file them with the board. There is a provision that the filing of them with the board under certain conditions operates automatically as approval. That is what the former member of the railway commission desires to say.
Implied approval.

Yes, that is true; but
that does not get away from the fact that in essence filing is essential in order that there may be objection, if desired.
Yes.
That is the fair way of putting it.
That is correct.

That is, the law contemplates equality of shippers under the conditions mentioned in the act, and that variations in the tariff rates under the four classifications provided., leaving out the special one, are open to action being taken, if any aggrieved person desires to take such action, after they are filed with the board. I think that is a fair statement of it.
I think so.

That being so, we are
certainly encroaching upon that rule-and nobody denies it. The only question therefore is this-

For good
cause.
But that is the point.
For good cause.

The whole question is a simple one: In the public interest are we warranted in departing from the rule which has been established during these years, and which resulted from the inquiry to which I directed attention the other day, and which I am not now going to repeat. That is the sole question-whether or not as a matter of high public policy we are warranted in departing from the existing law, which came into being because of abuses which existed
before its application. That is the story, and I think no one will deny that it is a fair statement.
But we are not departing from it.

The hon. member for Outremont says we are not departing from it. I only desire to point out that if the English language means anything we certainly are departing from it. Peradventure it does not mean what it says. But if it means we are departing from it, as my friend yonder says, for what good cause? I prefer to regard it as having been * departed from, and I am not unmindful of the reasons which are given as to why it should .be, and the force of those reasons. But to say the existing law is not departed from it is to do violence to one's understanding of the language. I will not do more than direct attention to these words:
Notwithstanding anything in the Railway Act-
And I have referred to the section in the Railway Act.
-or in this act-
The transport bill.
-a carrier-
And a carrier is defined by this measure as being a carrier to whom the act applies-I believe those are the exact words.
By rail, water or air.

Yes, I just wished to have the exact words, and I find that-
"carrier" means any person engaged in the transport of goods or passengers for hire or reward to whom this act applies, and shall include any company which is subject to the Railway Act.
That is, it includes every company which is organized as a railway company by act of this parliament. That is fundamental.
We go a step farther and provide that the carrier, as thus defined-
-may make such charge or charges for the transport of the goods of any shipper or for the transport of any part of his goods as may be agreed between the carrier and that shipper.
And approved by the board.

Just a minute. "As may be agreed to between the carrier and that shipper." Obviously that is contractual. That is, the carrier is authorized to make a contract with a shipper to carry his freight at any rate that may be agreed upon. But there is a limitation to that. That is the broad statement of the principle, but, the limitation is:
Provided that any such agreed charge shall require the approval of the board-
Transport Commission

Then there is the further provision:
-and the board shall not approve such charge if, in its opinion, the object to be secured by the making of the agreement can, having regard to all the circumstances, adequately be secured by means of a special or competitive tariff of tolls under the Railway Act or this act.
I hope the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Vien) and the minister consider themselves as being answered. It states distinctly in the bill that you shall not use this provision unless you cannot attain your end under the present law. That is said so distinctly that it does not admit of any doubt.
I always admitted that.

From what my hon. friend said this afternoon I gathered he thought differently. I felt that the hon. member for Outremont had not those words specifically in his mind. If under the existing law you can accomplish your end, then the matter will not be considered at all by the board. In other words, when you come to the board with your case, if it falls within the four comers of the Railway Act. the board must say, "You depart; we will have nothing to do with you on that basis under this act."
That means that the competitive rates would degenerate into a rate war.

Talk of a rate war is quite beside the question. I hope my hon. friend will permit me to say that without being offensive. I think on reconsideration he will hardly admit the possibility of a rate war arising under the present law.
The publication of a competitive rate might not have any particular effective result, because the highway carrier might publish a lower rate.
The highway carrier does not enter into this picture.
He does.
You must keep in mind the fact that the highway carrier does not enter into this picture.
That is what the law was made for.

The point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) was that we have not in any sense endeavoured to occupy that field. This legislation does not touch that. The minister nods his acquiescence. We are not in that field, and I ask my hon. friend to keep that in mind.
We are not in that field because it is a constitutional field. We cannot go there.

I hope my hon. friend does not conclude that I am suggesting that we should. This provision of the bill has given me much concern. It leaves it open to one of a group of carriers in a competitive territory to destroy the agreed rate.
How is that?

Let me read the section:
-and provided further that when the transport is by rail from or to a competitive point or between competitive points on the lines of two or more carriers by rail the board shall not approve an agreed charge unless the competing carriers by rail join in making the agreed charge.
If one carrier holds out, there is no agreed charge.
That is correct.
Surely my hon. friend did not mean that.

That was not in the English act, but it is put in so that we would not contravene the provisions of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, which calls on the roads to cooperate. We do not wish to start rate competition between the two railways.

At Vancouver you would have the competition of the Great Northern, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. If one of these three railroads does not agree to the agreed charge, then it is useless.
Then you cannot have an agreed charge.
Exactly. I point that out to my hon. friend from-I cannot think of his constituency.
It is Laurier, a very nice name.

I assure my learned and hon. friend that he does great credit to it I do not think the minister intended to destroy the value of this statute or the value of the agreed charge at a competitive point by making it possible for one of a group of competitive carriers to stand out and make an agreed charge impossible. The interest of that competitive carrier might be very limited because of the territory which it serves, but it can make an agreed charge impossible. That is the situation as I see it. Is it a matter of practical wisdom and of high national policy to introduce a provision for agreed charges with those limitations? I am not unmindful of the effect that highway transport has had upon the traffic of the

Transport Commission
railways. All you havre to do is to read the briefs which I am sure the minister received in this morning's mail.
Lewis Duncan.
He certainly must be an eminent authority; for he has been considered by this government on more than one occasion as being well worthy of his hire.
An eminent counsel.

My learned and hon.
friend describes him as an eminent counsel.
I assume that these briefs have been given the minute consideration that the minister thinks desirable. There is one saving provision in this bill, that is that it shall not come into force until proclaimed. If as a result of the investigation being carried on in Ontario in connection with highway traffic the minister is satisfied that it would not be in the national interest to proclaim it, I assume he will not do it. As it stands now, we are being asked to provide that a carrier and a shipper may make a contract for the transport of goods at a rate which encroaches upon the generally established rate of the country. It is further provided that that rate shall not be effective unless it is approved by the board, and further that it shall not be approved by the board if it is possible to secure the objective by other existing means. Lastly, it is provided that one of a group of carriers can destroy the contract by simply saying that he will not agree. I submit that that does not mean much. I first felt the encroachment was very great, but after reading the limitations I felt it wa.s very small. After reading the two together I feel it means nothing because it puts it in the hands of one of a group of competitors to destroy the agreement entirely; and I can conceive of such a situation being possible, although it might not be probable.
One thing further was said which I think on reflection the member for Kootenay East would regard as being too broad a statement. There is no right for anybody whose interests may be affected to be heard in a court of law unless he is a party to the transaction, and as we have not legislated with respect to the transport of goods on the highways such a carrier is not a party to the transaction and has no right to be heard in the court. Only recently in England in an important case in which a witness gave evidence and named half a dozen people in rather uncomplimentary terms it was suggested to the judge that these people had a right to be heard, but the judge decided that no witness lias a right to be heard in a court of law if he is not a party to the transaction. The judge laid
that down as the law. So my hon. friend's statement is too broad. This would be a correct statement of it, that you cannot deny to any party who has an interest in and is a party to the transaction the right to be heard in the courts. Every day decisions are made which affect the right of individuals who are not in the court but who are bound as a result of what has been decided in the court. The right of the truck owner to appear in the court is a right that does not attach unless he is brought into the court. The only people in the court here are the carriers under this act, and they are the only people who could be in the court unless we enlarge the field, which we have not done, in respect to highway traffic. Then the opportunity would be afforded for them to be heard.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that on balance, with the limitations imposed, I cannot bring myself to think that it is sound to encroach upon the rule, which has behind it such a body of public opinion and of decisions as we have both in the United States and here.
I pointed out the other day, and I am not going to do it again, the difference between conditions that prevail in Great Britain and here. They are so well defined that it is hardly necessary to do more than mention them for the differences to be at once appreciated. In England the field is divided into four strips of territory, if I might use that phrase; it is not very sound to institute a comparison between dissimilar things if you hope to arrive at any rule, and conditions in Great Britain and Canada are so dissimilar that I do not think you could arrive at any helpful conclusion by making the comparison. But knowing what I do of the history of the interstate commerce commission and of our own railway board, and knowing the time that was taken and the investigations that were made for the purpose of establishing the rule, I feel that we are taking a very great chance by providing for this encroachment upon that rule, which was a salutary one and worked out well, unless indeed at the same time we establish by adequate means jurisdiction over transport on the highway. Every province makes some regulations with respect to highway traffic. It is true that the regulations differ with the attitude of mind of the legislators of the nine provinces.
And none applies to rates.

So far as I know, none applies to rates, but regulations have been applied as to the weight of the car. having regard to the safety of bridges, also with respect to the effect on the asphalt or the surface of the road itself. They have also

Transport Commission
exercised control in some of the western provinces to a very great degree, as, for instance, to those who might be licensed or regulated for the handling of traffic in. a particular area. They went as far as 'that in one case, in a sparsely settled district in the far northern part of the country.
I think, Mr. Chairman, with the limitations as they read, the possibilities of the legislation being innocuous are very great. When the bill was first before the house and I read it. it had not that addition to the first part of section 35 which it now contains, but even with that I still think the minister is taking the proper course in providing that the act shall not go into effect until it is proclaimed, after he has satisfied himself by every means in his power as to just what will be involved if we make this encroachment upon a rule which I believe was salutary, which came into being because of great abuses, and a return to which we cannot as a Canadian people contemplate without realizing that the practices which prevailed before the interstate commerce commission or the railway commission came into being are not such as we can again tolerate in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I have very little comment to make, except to say that the provision referred to by my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) that the railways must act as a unit in making agreed charges is not a very serious curtailment. For many years the railway board has been the rate-making body for the railways, and it is the intention that it shall continue to be so. It is felt that it is not in the public interest for railways competing with each other to make special contracts, and the provision is there for that reason.
Amendment (Mr. Stevens) negatived. Subsection 1 of section 35 agreed to.
On section 35, subsection 4-Board approval of agreed charge.

Subsection 4 was allowed to stand for further examination. It has since been examined. It is an exact copy of the English act. The board of railway commissioners have been questioned regarding it, and it is felt that this is a desirable clause to have, taking into consideration the actual machinery of the board.
It defines the discretionary powers of the board within which they may grant their consent.
Quite.

Subsection agreed to.
Section 35 agreed to.

On section 37-Rights preserved. R.S., c. 79 Crowsnest Pass agreement.

The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) objected that the wording "or by chapter five of the statutes of 1897," which was the original Crowsnest Pass agreement, was not comprehensive enough to cover extensions of the Crowsnest Pass agreement since that time. I contend, and our solicitors contend, that the reference to the Crowsnest Pass agreement has no point in this act, because nothing in this act can possibly violate its provisions. But in order to meet the objection raised I will ask my colleague the Minister of Public Works to move that clause 37 be amended by striking out the words "or by chapter five of the statutes of 1897", in line 8 and substituting therefor the following words:
or by paragraph (e) of section 1 of chapter 5 of the statutes of Canada 1897, as extended and saved by subsection 5 of section 325 of the Railway Act.
I move accordingly.

I am sure the minister did not draft that. It is the first time I have ever seen salvation provided for by act of parliament. Had not the minister better say "preserved"? "Extended and preserved" would be better than "extended and saved".

If the chairman will make
that change, it is all right with me.

The amendment is:
that the word "saved" be deleted and the word "preserved" substituted therefor.
"Preserved" as in strawberry jam.

TURNER VALLEY OIL FIELDS: PROPOSED DUMPING DUTY ON MONTANA CRUDE-GERHARD NATURALIZATION CERTIFICATE- STATEMENT OF MR.
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire to bring to the attention of the house before we proceed

Turner Valley Oil Fields
with supply a matter of some considerable importance to the part of the country in which I live.
The development of the oil fields of southern Alberta has proceeded very slowly. It is thirty-three years ago this fall since I organized a company for the purpose of searching for natural gas and oil in what has since become the Turner valley field. We made a discovery of what was known as crude naphtha and of large quantities of natural gas in which naphtha was held in suspension in globules, and it proved to be very valuable from the standpoint not only of the gas being used for illuminating and domestic purposes in Calgary and other communities, tout also of the resultant oil which was taken by a process of refining, under which process the naphtha held in suspension was utilized. There have been continued borings and drillings in that area until at last large quantities of crude petroleum have been discovered at a depth in some instances of ten thousand feet or more. Anyone who has had to do with the drilling of a hole two miles into the earth's crust must realize something of the difficulties that have to be overcome and the risks incidental to the work, apart altogether from the cost, and will perhaps understand why so many years have passed since the first effort was made.
The discoveries that have been now made establish beyond question the fact that we have there an extremely valuable oil field. A very large number of oil wells have been sunk in that field. The so-called Turner valley has a width of approximately one mile; the length of field is at least sixteen miles, and perhaps a good deal more. During the last eighteen months or two years wells of increasing importance have been brought into production; wells have been drilled with a production of three and four thousand barrels of crude petroleum per day. But obviously, as is the case with many things we have in western Canada, we are confronted with great difficulties. The immediate market provided by a few people is of course limited. To lift crude oil over the Rocky mountains by means of a pipe line is a highly expensive process, if not an impossible one. It is not difficult to contemplate a pipe line of sufficient length to carry crude petroleum from the Turner valley oil fields to tidewater in British Columbia. Inasmuch, however, as the Turner valley is about half a mile in altitude, and the point in the Rockies over which it would be necessary to pass, unless one went south or north a great distance, is nearly a mile above sea level, it
follows that the crude petroleum would have to be lifted-and I used the word "lift" advisedly-nearly half a mile, which is almost prohibitive from the standpoint of mere cost.
Then the question arises as to the market in eastern Canada, where the population is.. To carry crude oil from Turney valley east to Fort William would involve the expenditure of many millions of dollars, and it would also involve a pipe line which would constantly have within it perhaps a million barrels of oil. That is a tremendous quantity. A pipe line of sufficient diameter and of the required length from Turner valley to Fort William therefore means the rendering unsalable for a time of a very large quantity of oil. When you reach the head of the lakes your troubles have only then begun, because the refineries in the east are to be found at Halifax, Montreal, Toronto and in other communities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sarnia.

The very large one at Sarnia is served by pipe line from the midcontinent field. Under the circumstances I think it is apparent to those who have been operating in western Canada in the Turner valley that they cannot hope, for instance, to displace crude oil coming from Colombia, Venezuela or Peru. That crude oil coming from those points is waterborne. It comes to Halifax, Montreal, Vancouver; and *wherever you have waterborne crude oil it is quite obvious that we could not hope, from an inland community like Turner valley, to ship our oil to compete with these importations. But there is what is known as the mid-continent field, and that extends north as far as Montana. It was because we could never be convinced that the forty-ninth parallel shut off oil discoveries that there was continued prospecting in the hope of one day getting oil in volume, because just south of us at Montana there has been a large field of oil which has been constantly operated during the last few years and which has supplied a substantial quantity of crude that has come into Canada. That is not carried in by pipe line. It is brought in by trucks and tank cars. The average truck carries something like forty barrels. The largest shipment that came to our country in any recent day from the Montana fields was ninety-five truckloads on May 23 last-that is last month-but the average, as I understand, has been something like thirty-five trucks per day. Since the discovery of crude in large quantities at Turner valley, there has been a constant reduction in the price at which Montana crude has been offered in western Canada.
Turner Valley Oil Fields

The price last week at which crude was being offered was as low as 80 cents per barrel, and contracts might have been made at a lower rate. In view of the fact that such importation limits to just that extent the use to which Turner valley crude can be put, those who are deeply concerned about the future of the industry in which they have invested their savings are strongly of the opinion that a dumping duty should be placed upon that product imported from Montana.
I am pointing out that there is no pipe line that conveys it across the country; it comes across in trucks. In the month of April last this country imported 51,523,000 gallons of crude oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is, all told.
Of that quantity, 37,635,000 gallons came from the United States; 6,924,000 from Colombia; 3,793,000 from Venezuela; and 3,748,000 from Peru.
But it does not say how much came from Montana.

I said from the United States, and Montana is a part of the United States. I said that the average quantity of Montana oil imported per day was thirty-five truckloads, that a truck carried forty barrels, and that the largest shipment of trucks had been ninety-five on May 23 last. The statistical record is not complete with respect to the rest of it, but I am making that statement in order to direct attention to the volume that is coming into this country from the United States, and I wish to follow that with this statement: It is not suggested at the moment that Turner valley is capable of satisfying all the requirements for crude oil of the Dominion of Canada; for roughly the daily requirements of crude oil in Canada are about 110,000 barrels, but apparently it is within sight, for during the present year, if the wells now under drilling are completed and produce as do existing wells, we shall in that valley be taking out of the earth 100,000 barrels of oil a day, if a market can be secured. The fact that the market is not available necessitates pro-rating, as it is called, the production from the wells; and inasmuch as there is no pipe line and only rail transport at the present moment to carry crude east, it follows that there has been, as additional wells have come into existence, a reduction in the quantity taken from each. That is the net result of pro-rating the production. The more wells, the less the quantity to be taken per day from each to supply the requirements.
Recently the wells owned by those who have expended substantial sums of money on

them have come into production, with the result that the pro-rating as provided for ,by regulation of Alberta has reduced the quantity taken from each, and the company that has a large number of wells is, of course, still producing in substantial volume, although each well is on the same relative pro rata basis. The request with respect to dumping duty arises out of the circumstances to which I have alluded; but the request that a duty be imposed upon the raw product is the complement of what I have just said with respect to pro-rating the output of those wells. And before the budget is delivered I am directing the attention of the government to these circumstances in order that, if it is thought well in the public interest, some action may be taken along the lines I have suggested.
But I want to go a step further. Some time ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) referred the matter to the tariff board and the board went west and made investigations. So fas as is known, the tariff board has made no report, and some of the Canadians who have been operating in that valley are very resentful that no action is being taken, and have expressed themselves in rather strong language. For instance, they refer to us in this parliament in terms which I hope will not be regarded as highly offensive:
The Canadian tariff hoard "investigates" the Turner valley situation and adjourns forever. In Ottawa 245 costly politicians talk for five months and accomplish nothing.
That is from an Alberta newspaper.
Yes, that is an extract from an editoral in The Albertan.
Sent to every member of the house.

I did not know that;
I thank my hon. friend. That shortens the need for my observations, because I see that my learned and hon. friend has already lead it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was sent to every hon. member.
Yes, the hon. member just observed that it was sent to every hon. member. That of course does not in any sense lessen its value.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it would be impossible to lessen its value.
Well, I do not look upon the matter in just that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That kind of comment I do.

I am not so sure that having regard to my observation of the government of this country for the last five months one is not warranted in making that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It says that 245 members of parliament talk too much. My right hon. friend is one of them.
Of course he is. But it rests with the government of the day to take the initiative. It is their job to see that something is done, for they only can expend money.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is too much talking.
They alone can take steps in regard to the tariff. They are the only ones who can deal with a dumping duty; they only can deal with unemployment, they only can deal with relief. What have they done?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Listened to speeches.
Well, they have been poor listeners; for the Prime Minister has not been in this house an average of an hour and a half a day since the session opened.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not fair.
It is as fair as it was to say it about me when I was Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Prime Minister is tired and has not been well for a few days. I do not think this remark was called for. We did not do the same to my right hon. friend.

You did not? Read the record. Day after day, week after week you referred to the fact that I was not in my place, because I was working long hours on work that I had to do. Now I say that the Prime Minister has not been in his place in this parliament on the average an hour and a half a day since it opened. Let there be no misunderstanding. Hon. members may have had to listen to speeches, and what is more, they may have to listen to more. One thing is perfectly clear, we have been here for five months and done nothing for the public good.
You have talked a lot.
What else was there to do? What was the government doing? It was the duty of the government to produce its program.
I am sure your government would satisfy the hungry people.

Do not let us talk about hunger. Just think of it! One hon. member, not here, saying that if you be hungry in Saskatchewan do not think of voting for this government. Do not think of voting for this government. If you be hungry think what will happen if you do not vote for the Patterson government. That is what the hon. member for Regina, (Mr. McNiven) has been stating to the people of this country, according to the public press. And the resources of civilization seem to be in striking evidence in various sections of that fair province.
I recall a statement, "I shall cure unemployment or perish in the attempt."

Well, the hon. member may regard that as a clever observation. The employment that existed at the time we came into office vanished but was replaced by increased unemployment; what is more, we did perish in the attempt, and that is what will happen to this administration. No one ever heard a single regret expressed by me at any action the electors might take with respect to it. That was not the statement that was made; it has to be taken with the context that surrounded it. If hon. members will read what was said before 1935, if they will look at the hoardings, look at the picture of the nine provinces, if they look at the unity of then and now they will understand something about conditions. Look at Canada today, the federal power in Vancouver a joke; the fact held up to the eyes of all the world that the dominion's own property cannot be safeguarded by the Canadian people. You find that Alberta is now conducting the affairs of the nation. There is no national government; it is just what each province says.
Has this any connection with the dumping duty on oil?
Nova Scotia is still sane.

Now, I have been
diverted from my theme. I was pointing out that the tariff board was considering this question.

Pour
some oil on the troubled waters.
Yes, but remember that the products of oil are highly inflammable. A spark sometimes ignites them, and even the vapour is a source of large quantities of power.

Louder.
Turner Valley Oil Fields
Oh well, it is unimportant that my hon. friend should hear me.
I always like to hear the leader of the opposition because mostly he speaks sound common sense.

I was pointing out that the tariff board had had this matter under consideration and investigation. What I want to know is whether or not some steps can be taken without delay to ensure that this hard-won product may be utilized in this country by Canadians instead of importations being continued within the area served by this field. I am not foolish enough to suggest that Turner valley oil can serve the wants of Halifax, or even of Vancouver at the moment, but I am suggesting that this tariff board could make a report without delay, and that the government, before the budget is brought down, can deal adequately with it.
On another occasion it may be necessary for me to make some observations with respect to another aspect of the matter, but at the moment I content myself-not expecting that the government is going to announce a remedy at the moment; far from it-with saying that before the budget is delivered the government have the fullest possible opportunity for determining what action should be taken. Because it must be remembered that petroleum is one of the greatest producers of new wealth in a country. As soon as a well is in production new wealth becomes available. You do not have to wait three or four years as with the growing of cattle or sheep; you get your new wealth at once. It is for that reason that I direct the attention of the government to this matter, in the very earnest hope that they will take steps to remedy the situation, in order that the market which is available in that area-a very limited one,
I am quite frank about it-may become available for Canadian products.
One step further. It must be in the mind of the government that we had on the statutes of Canada for I think a quarter of a century an act providing for giving a bonus for the production of petroleum. I dare say there are many hon. members who have forgotten that entirely. If that provision were in force today it would involve the payment of very large sums of money. It was repealed because it was thought that the country could not stand the strain if large quantities of oil were discovered, but it was utilized for many years in Ontario. Now they do not ask a bonus, but they ask for assistance if need be in transport. I happen to know that the railway companies are giving the matter consideration, to see whether they cannot get

the traffic rather than involve the country and the companies in the construction of pipe lines. It is for that reason that I have ventured, before we proceed with supply, to bring this matter to the attention of the house, although I may possibly do so at greater length on another occasion.
One other matter I wish to speak of, and that is to direct the attention of the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) to what I conceive to be the very urgent necessity of appointing a commissioner under the Naturalization Act to investigate the activities of Mr. Gerhard. I have received a detailed report from Edmonton, and from another section of this country within the last few days; I do not desire to prejudge in any sense the case of any person, but I do think that on the evidence that can be established, for him to have a certificate of naturalization as a British subject at the present time does violence, and great violence indeed, to my understanding of the requisites of British citizenship.
I shall be glad to place in the possession of the Secretary of State details of evidence which have come to me and which will enable him, I believe, if he will be good enough to appoint a commissioner without delay, to make an investigation which will satisfy him that the outstanding certificate of naturalization should be cancelled without further delay. I say that this action should be taken if the evidence proves to be in accordance with the information which I have.
I desire to make it abundantly clear that I have no wish to prejudge anyone's case or to make any declaration as to the value to be attached to the evidence in question.

Mr. Speaker, I have tremendous respect and deep regard for the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), but I shall have to disagree with him. I am sorry I had not known the matter was to be discussed, and also sorry that for a few moments the discussion turned into a political sabre fight, which got us exactly nowhere. I do know that many hundreds, perhaps thousands, of farmers between Lethbridge and Medicine Hat and the international boundary have tractors equipped to use Montana crude oil. It is a type of crude oil which can be burned directly in tractors, whereas the crude which in the past has been produced in the Turner valley has not been a type as easily consumed or as economically used. I know that many farmers in southern Alberta are using Montana crude oil, which they bring in at a cheap rate.

Turner Valley Oil Fields
They haul it in off seasons of the year, and store it in concrete storage tanks below the ground. That would account for the importation of thousands of barrels to which the right hon. gentleman referred.
While it may be considered that opposition by the farmers to a dumping duty, for the reasons put forward by the leader of the opposition, would be selfish, I suggest that their particular case should be adequately presented to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the government before any steps are taken. Furthermore, I am sure the Minister of Finance will agree with me when I say that while the dumping duty need not generally raise the price of crude oil or fuel in the west, past history and experience would tell us that it likely would have that effect. Goodness knows that gasoline and all other fuel products in western Canada, where there is an abundance of raw products, are selling at unconscionably high prices, for no really good reason. If we impose a duty to overcome the pro-ration in the Turney valley, or to offset the effect of the small importations by trucks, I believe, without having made a thorough study of the matter, that much more harm than good would be done, and I hope the government will keep that phase of the matter firmly in mind before making any change of the kind suggested by the right hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I must add my word of protest against the suggestion of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he asks that a dumping duty be imposed on crude oil entering Canada. I oppose the suggestion because I believe such action would increase the price of crude oil in Canada. I have the further reason that only recently in the city of Portage la Prairie a cooperative oil refining plant has been built, and I believe I am right in saying that such a tariff change would increase the difficulty of that cooperative. They would have to pay more for their raw materials.
I am not suggesting that they pay more.

Perhaps not, but I believe from experience we can safely say that a dumping duty would have that effect. I raise my voice in order to make sure that in connection with any question of this kind the crude oil requirements of the cooperative refineries shall be considered before any dumping duty is imposed.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) : Mr. Speaker, I had no advance notice of this matter being raised, and therefore I have to speak entirely from memory with regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not criticizing anyone, but am merely excusing myself if any statement I may make should be incomplete.
I will endeavour to be sure that it will not be inaccurate.
With regard to charging the government with inaction in the matter, I do not think any of the producers in the Turner valley will join in such a charge. When last year the new production of the Turner valley first became certain the problems apparently arising in connection with that production were brought to the attention of the government by the producers' association in the Turner valley. They asked a thorough investigation into a situation which would be created by the development of a heavily producing oil field in Alberta.
There was a question as to what body available to the government would be best suited to conduct such an investigation. Obviously transportation questions were involved, but transportation questions were not by any means the whole problem. Problems of marketing were involved, but they did not constitute the whole problem. It seemed that there might conceivably be a tariff aspect to the problem. Personally I regard the tariff aspect as relatively unimportant in relation to the problem presented by the increased production in the Turner valley. I am willing to be convinced from evidence that my view in that regard is wrong, but that was the view I held when the parties concerned came to the government to discuss the matter.
In any event the government decided that in view of all the circumstances the tariff board was the body best fitted to look into the matter, partly because of the mass of information which was available to the tariff board as a result of its previous investigation of the tariff on gasoline and oil products generally, and partly because in Judge Sedgewick we knew we had a man who would use that information in order to extract everything possible on the subject which might be of service to the interested parties.
The inquiry proceeded. I think everyone connected with it will agree that although no report has been made, the results of the inquiry have been distinctly beneficial to those concerned. As a result of the inquiry as far as it
Turner Valley Oil Fields

proceeded negotiations have occurred between the producers and the railways and between the producers and the oil refiners which have materially improved conditions. The improvement has not been sufficient to eliminate the problem. I do not claim that for a moment; but there came a time in the progress of the investigation when it became apparent that the important thing to learn was: What is the potential volume of production from the Turner valley wells? If my memory serves me aright, in the early months of this year the Alberta government indicated that they were making a further test of potential production, but the hearings had reached the point where the independent producers' association requested the board to adjourn sine die. Those words have a bearing on the editorial that was read.
