speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hearings of the
tariff board were postponed indefinitely at the request of the producers of the Turner valley speaking as an organized body. Within the last two weeks the results of the tests of the potential production of existing wells have become available. I am speaking from memory, but I believe I am correct when I say that the potential production of the existing wells is 37,000 barrels a day. At the time the hearings were postponed it was known that the consumption within that area of Canada which could be economically served from the Turner valley was approximately 15,000 barrels a day. The then known excess potential production over the

Turner Valley Oil Fields
15.000	barrel consumption was not sufficient warrant, in the opinion of the producers, for the tariff board to continue investigating the matter with any hope of producing a constructive suggestion.
The situation has now changed. Within the last two weeks it has become apparent that
37.000	barrels a day is the potential of the existing wells. My right hon, friend speaks of other wells which are in the process of development and which will raise that potential to about 100,000 barrels a day.
I said it was believed that if they maintained the same rate of development, by the end of the year they would be getting 100,000 barrels a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I point out that in connection with this increased volume of production this parliament and this government do not control the extent to which the Turner valley field shall be developed. This government and this parliament cannot determine whether the Turner valley shall be permitted to produce 37,000 barrels, 50,000 barrels or 100,000 barrels a day. That power and that right are in the legislature and the government of Alberta. We have for the first time in Canada the problem which has been the most difficult one that the oil producing industry in the United States has had to contend with during the past number of years. In every one of the oil producing states it has been a matter of serious difficulty, first, to control the degree of development in order to prevent every one from being flooded with oil which could not be sold at a satisfactory price and, second, to pro-rate the existing wells at a point which would be fair to everyone. For the information of hon. members from other parts of Canada, may I point out again that the control of the rate of production is in the province of Alberta, not in this parliament.
And is being exercised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says that it is being exercised. I believe there are measures in effect in Alberta looking to that control. Looking for oil is so indefinite, so far as results are concerned, that when control measures become necessary, they are seldom effective. That has been the history of the oil fields in the south. During the last two weeks Mr. Frawley, an official of the attorney general's department of the Alberta government, and who, I believe, represented the government during the tariff board inquiry, has been in communication with the chairman of the board with respect to the new development. The producers' organization has also 51952-230
been in communication with the board with respect to the new development. The last advice I received was that the producers' organization was meeting to-day in Calgary in order to determine what further steps it would be wise to take, having regard to the fact that the inquiry was adjourned on their own request just a short time ago.
A short time ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not very long. I have not the date in mind, but speaking from memory, I believe it was two or three months ago. I give this information to the house for the purpose of indicating that the government is alive to the fact that there is a real problem in connection with the development of an extensive oil field in that part of Canada, the capacity of which to consume oil is readily ascertainable as being considerably below the potential productive capacity of the wells now being developed. I hardly think it is fair, however, to lay at the door of this parliament the responsibility for finding a market for an unlimited quantity of oil produced under conditions of geographical difficulty so far as its distribution is concerned. In that connection I would point out that it is not a question of losing the oil because it is not taken out of the ground to-day or to-morrow. It is merely a question of so organizing as to enable that wealth to flow into consumption at a rate which will best serve the interests of both the producers and the consumers of that wealth. The oil does not disappear because it is left in the ground. If it is not taken out to-day, it is still there to-morrow. I do not think anyone who has studied the Alberta oil formation will assume that it is at all likely that oil is being drained from the Turner Valley formation into any other formation which would permit it to be taken out of the ground, for instance, in a foreign country. There is no evidence of that.
The question then is merely one of how fast shall the oil be taken out of that reservoir which is in the Turner Valley. Those people who have drilled wells and put their savings into them, as my right hon. friend has suggested, are certainly entitled to and ought to have consideration because the adventuring of savings in the great enterprise of digging holes two miles into the ground without knowing whether or not you are going to get anything out is something we need to encourage in Canada. But I submit seriously that we should not put this question upon the ground of the national necessity of finding a market for an unlimited production of oil.

I was very careful to
say that.

Turner Valley Oil-Fields

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is far better, as geological knowledge advances and as we get a better idea of how much oil is in that great pool in the Turner Valley, that we or the government of Alberta, or possibly both of us, should carefully consider measures to conserve the production of oil in that field on luch a basis that the daily production will ensure its continuing to serve economically the people of those parts of Canada which can be served by it to the very best advantage.
In the meantime we have the problem of dealing with the present production. I do not believe that my right hon. friend's suggestion of a dumping duty with respect to that small quantity of oil which is coming in from Montana would have a hairbreadth of influence with respect to this great problem involved in a production of 37,000 barrels a day, which may possibly rise, as he himself says, to 100.000 barrels a day. I have no knowledge of the precise quantities that come over the Alberta border from Montana. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Mitchell) spoke of the effect of a dumping duty on the farmers who use the oil. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) spoke of another phase of the same matter. These factors must all be taken into consideration. But I do not believe that a dumping duty is a solution, although certainly the tariff board must take into account in their inquiry the effect on our national well-being of what is happening in the way of oil coming over in truckloads from Montana, and I feel sure that due regard will be given by the board to what the facts in the case reveal in that regard.
The question seems to me to be one of whether Canada can find some means of transporting oil over what are known to be uneconomic distances in order to find a market. The question is: Is it better to hold down present production in Alberta and thus continue the life of that oil field over a longer period of time, or is it the better course to enter into some artificially assisted means of getting the oil into a wider market than is at present economically available to it? I know I am merely posing the problem; I am not suggesting an answer to it, nor did my right hon. friend do so. I believe he put forward the dumping duty not as a serious answer to the problem, but just as one of the incidental features of it. I think he will agree, after hearing what has happened in connection with the matter, that the government has
 moved as reasonably as was possible under the circumstances; that the machinery provided for investigating this matter is the best that is available, and that the investigation is proceeding in a normal and reasonable manner to accomplish the end in view.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not be long in what I have to say. May I at the outset express my 
appreciation of the courtesy which has been displayed in connection with the debate on this bill, as it was displayed in the debate on the bill introduced in 1934.
I intend to vote for the bill. I respect the opinions of hon.. members, and of people outside the house. It is my view that if it is necessary either to repeal or to amend section 236 of the criminal code to make the bill effective, then for many reasons that action should be taken. I have received quite a number of communications concerning the proposed amendment, but I shall not take the time of the house to repeat all that has been said. I believe the whole story was outlined in 1934 after a. sweepstakes measure had passed both houses in the province of Quebec and the Canadian Senate, but was afterwards rejected by the House of Commons.
As a life governor of a hospital in the city of Verdun, and being familiar with needs for hospitalization, I can say that I believe something should be done for the support of hospitals. I am well aware that there are conscientious objectors whose opinions I respect. Nevertheless we must all realize that each year large sums of money are sent to help hospitals in Ireland or Australia, or to a veterans' association in Newfoundland. To obtain the moneys prizes are offered in connection with the Cambridgeshire handicap, the Derby, or some other sporting event. That is a logical procedure to adopt.
To-day we are in the midst of gambling; there is no use in hiding the fact. I have no doubt that we should respect the opinions of those who conscientiously object to helping hospitals by means of sweepstakes. I would suggest, however, that if the hospitals do not *wish to take that money, it could be diverted to some other useful purpose. Some who buy tickets on sweepstakes or lotteries may do so in a gambling spirit, but I suggest that if they did not spend the money for that purpose they would spend it in slot-machines, bingo games, barbottes, or other gambling devices.
This is not a political or party issue, nor was it a political issue in 1934. While I served as alderman of the city of Verdun I became aware, as all hon. members must have done, that circuses, fairs, midways and shows come from other countries, bringing their animal acts, to divert the attention of the children and adults. We learn, however, that if they had no gambling devices in their organizations they would not dare to come. They come with the idea of making money and then taking it back to the United States or some other foreign country.

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes
I do not wish to enter into a discussion of foreign relations, but I do know that there are certain regulations set out by the Department of National Revenue with which fairs, shows or midways must comply. The agricultural and other societies sponsoring the shows are supposed to be bona fide. There must be conformity with forms 1914, B-18 and B-9. But the gambling devices are not included in those permits. If we are not to have lotteries or sweepstakes, then for heaven's sake let us not have circuses, shows and midways from other countries which come here with their gambling devices. Certainly those shows would not come if it were not for the gambling devices they carry.
I am glad this is not a political issue. I am urged to vote for the measure because I wish to help our institutions, and because I know that during June, July, August and September gambling devices do enter the country. Large amounts of money are wagered, and those sums are taken back to another country. Although I do not wish to speak at length, and should like to hear other hon. members -or have a vote taken, may I point out that last year in Verdun people were arrested because they were operating gold-digging machines which came from the United States. They come through the customs under the present arrangement. Are we to allow gambling in that form and then not permit the provinces to deal with this question as they see fit? I am not afraid to admit that people were arrested in Verdun for using these gambling devices. These machines came from the United States and were not subject to duty. All that is necessary to get them in is for the secretary of some agricultural fair to state that they are bona fide exhibits. But they were not; they were money-making machines. Are people to be allowed to come from the United States to make money with these gambling devices? I contend that we should amend the criminal code to legalize something which is now being done illegally.
If there are certain hospitals or educational institutions that do not wish to accept money in this form, that would be up to th:-m. Such funds could always be diverted to some other form of charity. We should be logical. I remember in 1934 when you, Mr. Speaker, introduced a bill to amend the criminal code in connection with lotteries, but the motion for second reading was negatived. Both the upper and lower houses of the legislature of Quebec have been unanimous in support of sweepstakes. We should try to do something
to alleviate the burden of taxes upon the business man. He is forced to pay taxes to support charitable institutions, baby clinics, girls' and boys' camps and so forth. As a great man told me this morning here, we are on the road to chaos.
I am ready to agree with those who contend that this is bad economy; nevertheless I contend that a law which tries to prohibit everything, sometimes prohibits nothing. The argument is put forth that the legalizing of sweepstakes and ' lotteries would decrease philanthropic contributions. I do not see it in that way. A philanthropist is a born philanthropist; if he has the means he is able to find plenty of opportunities to demonstrate his generosity. In Montreal the millionaire philanthropists do not grow like onions. This amendment would provide an opportunity for many people who otherwise would not do so to contribute toward the assistance of their fellow citizens. Many people would not make such a contribution unless it was in the nature of gambling. We seem to be entering an era of gambling at the present time. I am sure if I looked in the pockets of many of my colleagues I would find sweepstake and lottery tickets.
Section 92, subsection 7 of the British North America Act provides that the provinces shall have jurisdiction over the maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums and charitable institutions, other than marine hospitals. It is paradoxical to have section 92 state that each province shall look after the maintenance of hospitals, while section 236 of the criminal code forbids their adopting ways and means of doing so. Why should we do something illegal? If the criminal code is not amended, the man who wants to bet will have to change his name. He may be called Jules, like myself, and he would have to change his name to Juliette. He may be called Albert and he would have to change his name to Albertina. I do not approve that.
Bad economy, good economy, we have it in our hands to decide. The slot-machines are simply a racket. Bingo is a racket. Tombolas are a racket. Under section 18 of the Customs Act, five or more cars containing nothing but gambling devices would have to pay only $250 when entering Canada. If there were less than five cars, the rate would be $125. If it were not for the gambling devices that these people are permitted to bring across the boundary line, they would not come at all.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has introduced Bill No. 137, to amend the criminal code, which will be discussed at a later date.
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

This gambling device question will have to be settled to the satisfaction of all the people of this country. People should not be allowed to spend their money on these machines and then have that money go to another country. I understand that in 1934, one of the offices of the sweepstakes organization in Montreal sent $294,000 to the Irish hospitals.
As I said before, I respect the opinions of conscientious objectors, but we must remember that prohibition sometimes invites lawlessness, racketeering and profiteering.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from British Columbia, I think it might be well for me to make a few remarks on this bill because its mover (Mr. Bertrand, Laurier), has referred to that province as being favourable to sweepstakes. The vote to which the hon. member referred showed that only a very small minority of the people of the city of Vancouver and of British Columbia were in favour of sweepstakes, and I do not think the vote indicated for one moment that the people of British Columbia are favourable to an amendment to the criminal code to legalize sweepstakes in this country. In fact, since this debate opened I have received a large number of communications from my district on the subject of sweepstakes, and only one of them was in favour of this bill. I admit, however, that I am not in a position to state what percentage of the people of British Columbia are favourable to the bill, nor do I think my hon. friend is.
The ministerial association of my city communicated with the attorney general of British Columbia asking his stand on sweepstakes, and under date of April 14 last he replied, " I would certainly refuse to sanction anything of the kind." I am personally convinced that the legalizing of sweepstakes would not, both from a moral and an economic standpoint, be in the best interests of Canada. I should not like to see the lottery business made a department of provincial government, with the tickets backed by the dignity of the province. Some suggest we might sell the tickets in the United States, competing with the lotteries of the petty republics of South America.
There is another reason why I think no member from British Columbia could support this legislation. Without doubt, if this legislation passed and Ontario and Quebec took advantage of it, tickets would be put on sale in the smaller provinces, and the result would be that in a province like British Columbia, with a much smaller population,

our people would be contributing, not to our own institutions, but to those of the two larger provinces. So from that standpoint it would not be in the interests of the smaller provinces of Canada to support this legislation.
Great Britain and the United States have both had experience with agitations for legalizing lotteries and sweepstakes, and it is interesting to note that in reply to an agitation in recent years in Great Britain for reenacting legislation legalizing lotteries a commission was set up which inquired into the matter, and from its report I quote the following sentence:
The existing general prohibition in this country of all lotteries, whether promoted here or abroad, should be maintained, subject to the exemptions referred to below, and the law against foreign and illegal lotteries should be strengthened.
That was the commission's recommendation, and the law in Great Britain to-day makes it illegal in connection with any lottery in Great Britain or elsewhere:
. . . to print, sell, advertise, distribute tickets, or print or publish any description of a lottery or any prize-winners or winning tickets in one.
That is how the United Kingdom dealt with the agitation for the reestablishment of lotteries.
I do not think it is necessary for me to relate the experience of the United States. In 1834 lotteries were prohibited in that country after an experience over a number of years.
This bill comes before us, Mr. Speaker, clothed in righteousness. It is a little different from the bill before parliament some years ago in that it couples universities with hospitals. The last speaker (Mr. Wermenlinger) urged us to adopt this legislation in order to help hospitals, but I am convinced and I think every member of the house who has had any experience at all with sweepstakes realizes, that an individual purchases a sweepstake ticket not for the purpose of helping hospitals but for what he or she may get out of it. I am also convinced that the legalizing of lotteries and sweepstakes in Canada would not stop the sale in this country of the Irish sweepstakes tickets, because men and women who want to gamble would still pay $2.50 to buy a ticket with the chance of winning $150,000. It would not stop that for one minute.
Those of us who have had experience as public men know how often we are pressed to buy tickets for this, that and the other organization. Just imagine what it would be like if every province in Canada had a bunch of canvassers on the streets selling tickets for sweepstakes!

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes
A peculiar thing about this argument that the sweepstakes are for the benefit of hospitals is that I have not come across one hospital board that was in favour of raising its revenue from the sale of sweepstakes tickets. In March, 1928. a resolution was passed by the Canadian Hospital Council as follows:
That the Canadian Hospital Council cannot support the principle of raising funds by means of sweepstakes.
The British Hospital Association, which claims to be the heaviest loser through the Irish sweepstakes, passed the following resolution:
That the British Hospital Association is not in favour of an amendment of the law affecting public sweepstakes which purport to be for the benefit of voluntary hospitals.
And they go on to point out many reasons why, but I do not think it is necessary for me to repeat them here in detail.
One thing which I think we should consider very seriously is that these institutions, no matter where they may be located in Canada, must necessarily receive additional financial support in addition to the revenue derived from the care of patients. This should be provided through our legislatures and other public bodies. I am of the opinion that just as soon as you set up some gambling device to raise money for hospitals, you will find that the people who now subscribe will direct their donations to some other object.
The hospitals point out that it will be impossible to finance our hospitals by means of a sweepstake. The maintenance cost of our hospitals, excluding capital expenditure, amounted, according to the last Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures, to $41.405,86S for non-mental hospitals and S10.484.937 for mental hospitals, or a total maintenance cost of $51,890,805. The amount contributed by patients was $21,197,612, leaving a balance of $30,693,193, which bad to be raised from other sources. While some of this balance comes from nongovernmental sources, most of it is made up of the government and municipal share of hospital support. To meet this amount of $30,000.000. the annual amount required from the people, on the basis of the Irish srveepstakes would be $150,000,000. Were the full cost of maintenance to be met, as is anticipated by many, the total amount required would be still higher. The Irish commission, it is pointed out, has received applications for grants from but seventy-three hospitals, and has the English speaking world to draw from. Canada has some 969 hospitals, of which 608 are public and therefore would be eligible, and
would have to meet strong competition in selling tickets because of the huge prizes given elsewhere. The burden of supporting our hospitals would be shifted, to the extent of the sweepstakes contributions, to those least able to afford it. This has been repeatedly observed in Ireland, Spain and South American countries.
Let me repeat that I am convinced, after going thoroughly into this matter, as I think any hon. member would be who has followed the history of lotteries in other countries and the experience hospitals have had in regard to lotteries, that this legislation should not be enacted.
In speaking about the legislation I wish to refer to the bill that has been introduced. The bill was introduced and had its first reading on February 24, 1938. I find on my file two copies of the bill. The first bill introduced is the one that I think we are discussing,-the one which was introduced in the regular way, received its first reading and was up for second reading. But since May 9 another bill has been injected into the file, and it is altogether different. It has an explanatory clause and is underlined. That bill did not receive first reading in this house; it was not introduced in the regular way. So I wish to raise the point which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to in dealing with another bill on May 10. The Prime Minister at that time said:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, before we proceed any further, the rules of the house as adopted on June 14, 1923, among other provisions contain the following:
"In the text of the bill, on the left hand page, new matter shall be indicated by such typographical means as may best suit the varying circumstances of each case, such as brackets, italics, underlining, asterisks, etc. Opposite each clause, on the right hand page, the enactment amended thereby, or so much thereof as is essential, shall be printed with the proposed changes to be made therein similarly indicated."
I would point out that the bill which was introduced in the regular way and received the first reading does not contain the explanatory clauses to which the Prime Minister referred, and I contend that this bill is not in order.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Generally - National Gallery of Canada, $115,000.
Will the minister explain the increase?
The increase is to provide a larger sum for the trustees for the purchase of more works of art.

What is the sense of buying more works of art when there is not a building in which to display the ones they have now? They are all stored away, or at any rate a great many of the valuable paintings are, and the public never see them.

A number of these works of art are sent to the different provinces for exhibition purposes, and the trustees have not abandoned the idea that some day parliament will provide them with a suitable building in which to display all the works of art we possess.

This estimate affords me an opportunity to say something which I have wanted to say during the last four or five years but never had a chance until to-night to express. I cannot but think a number of Canadian artists are not adequately represented in the National Gallery. I feel strongly about this. The last time I visited the gallery and looked over the Canadian pictures I certainly found a dearth of pictures by one or two artists who, I believe, might fairly be classified as ranking Canadian artists. I am bound to say that there is one picture which has not impressed me as being authentic. It would seem to be regarded as Van Dyck, and while I am not at all an expert I am inclined to think that it might be well if the word "After" were placed before the name Van Dyck on that particular picture. There is a substantial number of Canadian artists who are not at all adequately represented in the gallery. On the last occasion on which I visited the gallery I tried to make effective my criticism of some pictures there, but I did not succeed. Certainly they do not dignify the National Gallery, whereas some of the paintings of those who are not represented would be an ornament to almost any gallery in the world. It would be unfair, of course, to particularize; for that might be regarded as unkind; but I make that observation to the minister, and I suggest that if he has an opportunity to visit the gallery he might see to what extent Canadian artists are represented there. If he does, I shall be glad to have a discussion with him as to what his convictions are in that regard.

I am very much inclined to agree with the words of the right hon. gentleman as to proper encouragement being given to Canadian artists. Not -being myself an art critic, I would not venture any opinion on the works of art there, though I must confess, even if I am a layman, that it is difficult to admit that certain works which are on exhibit in the gallery are masterpieces. I quite agree, however, that we should do all that we can to encourage Canadian artists as far as possible.

We have ample funds with which to purchase Canadian pictures. We have had the benefit of the services of excellent experts in the selection of old masters and of contemporaneous pictures as

Supply-Public Works-Harbours and Rivers
well. Some of the pictures that have been selected for us abroad are by men of great eminence and are permanent memorials to their greatness. About that there can be no doubt. We have works of most of the great artists, and I am not for a moment suggesting that we should limit our purchases. I must say, however, that I was disappointed-I put it in that way-when last I visited the gallery and looked over Canadian works. I do not think the display is a fair representation of the ability of Canadian painters; that is, those on exhibit. There may, however, be some put away that I have not been able to see.
Let me assure the minister that what I am saying does not refer particularly to his administration; in fact, it refers with equal, if not greater force, to the administration that preceded this. In my opinion, however, the principle is wrong of selecting merely a certain type of picture which apparently merits the approval of a certain type of mind but which does not commend itself to others. If we are to have representation of Canadian art, it should be not of one school only but of all schools, and as far as possible every worthy artist who has produced anything that merits a place in our National Gallery should be there. I suggest that no preconceived notions with respect to one school or one type of picture should prevail, but that all should find a place in the gallery. I admit that we have not produced many great pictures in this country, but at the 6ame time there are one or two of our artists who have achieved very fine landscape. Some have attained great eminence in the painting of trees, which is not easy work. I have seen one or two productions of an artist who happens to be employed in the civil service here, and whose pastel work is particularly good. Some of his water colours have high artistic qualities. In discussing this subject I did not intend to particularize at all but rather wanted to suggest that there should be in the gallery scope for the exhibition of works of every school and of every artist whose work is worthy of a place among the collections of the works of Canadian painters.

I will undertake to place the views of my right hon. friend before the trustees. In order to show the favourable disposition of the trustees, I may say that during the fall there was in the art gallery an interesting exhibition of Canadian design.

It is a far cry from the leader of the opposition to where I sit, and I am sorry to say I could not hear
a single word he said. But I gather from the reply of the minister that he was recommending an increase in the cultural development of our country, and the setting aside of moneys in order to assist Canadian artists and (he cultural development of Canada generally. These are the things that last. When we pass away these elements of art, whether carvings in stone or paint on canvas or music on paper, are the things which will be Canada. Unless we realize that even now, in our present hard-up condition, we must strive to perpetuate something of the conditions of our times, Canada will perish. We face westward with a blazoning on our peace tower of the words, "Where there is no vision the people perish." I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that $61,000 set aside for the acquisition of works of art is almost pusillanimous. If we consider the manner in which these things are cared for in other departments equally responsible for the protection of our culture, we ought to be ashamed. I sincerely hope the Minister of Finance and all others in the government will definitely determine to see that Canada is not backward in this matter.

Is there any portion of these amounts for the maintenance of the large cruisers found in some of the harbours, and especially the harbours of Ontario? From what I can gather they are used principally for week-end parties, and are of very little use for harbour control work.

Has any definite action
been taken in regard to the opening of Eagle Nest creek at Delta, Manitoba?
No.

I should like to remind the minister that over three hundred ratepayers and other people belonging to the Delta beach association feel that this matter is not receiving the attention it should receive. I made a trip to Ottawa last year and took the matter up with the deputy. The question is that there is a waterway across some privately owned land used by other people, and it is impossible for the Delta beach association or any other public body or individual to gain access to the public shooting grounds which have been set aside years ago by the Manitoba government.
That creek has been used for years and years. People get into their canoes and follow Eagle Nest creek to get to the shooting grounds. The man who owns the land, a wealthy man from Winnipeg, has put an obstruction across Eagle Nest creek, thereby shutting out the public from access to the public shooting grounds. The Manitoba government has refused to take any action, declaring that it was a matter for the dominion government, and that Eagle Nest creek was a navigable stream and therefore under the jurisdiction of the dominion government. That is why I made the trip to Ottawa to find out whether or not it was under the jurisdiction of the dominion government. My advice at that time was that it was a navigable stream; that orders would be issued to the man in question to remove the obstruction, and that if he did not remove it, the department would undertake to do so and charge the costs of removal to the man who owned the land.
The owner of the land refuses to move the obstruction, but he made the promise that if the dominion government would open the mouth of Eagle Nest creek, which owing to the low waters of lake Manitoba a few years ago, had filled with sand, he would be glad to remove the obstruction. So far as we know, the last letter was received from Mr. Hunter,' the deputy minister, on May 13, stating:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 12th instant, enclosing copy of a letter from Mr. R. H. Home of Portage la Prairie, Manitoba, secretary of the Delta beach association, concerning Eagle Nest creek.
The matter will be given the further consideration which you request, and you will be advised later what further action the department contemplates.
That is the last word we have.
In a letter from the secretary of the Delta beach association it is pointed out that if the creek continues to remain closed by the obstruction placed there by the private owner, the hunters and general public who wish to go to the shooting grounds would have to travel six and a half miles in order to reach those grounds, whereas they formerly ran their boats or canoes up Eagle Nest creek for a distance of only half a mile.

I have no doubt the minister got this estimate through council in the absence of the president of the council, who happens to be the Prime Minister. Olher-wise, surely he would never have managed to get an appropriation for an armoury in Hull. As the poet says:
And freedom shrieked-as Kosciusko fell!
What a shriek there must have been when the appropriation for this armoury went through, in view of the denunciation of armouries one heard on the radio in the fall of 1935. The minister will remember it.
I do not.
That settles it. That is how it got through.
I think we should have some explanation why this armoury is being built in Hull, costing the taxpayers of this country $270,000. Why is it being built? I want to know something about it.
How many regiments are housed in it?
Where are the antimilitarists?
I want an explanation of this item.

It houses the Hull Regiment, including the headquarters company and four rifle companies, with a total strength of all ranks of 470. The request came from the regiment itself and those interested in its welfare, and was approved by the National Defence department.
It is just half a regiment.
The amount of the re vote would indicate that $16,500 was spent last year; on what was that spent?
We paid $10,000 for a site. In addition, advertising for tenders, legal services and architect's fees account for the expenditure of $16,500.
An outside architect was employed?
Yes.
Who was he?

Mr. Bournet, of Hull.

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
What is the size of the site, because $10,000 seems a pretty substantial amount to pay for a site, if I know where this armoury is?
The size is twenty-one acres.

Item agreed to.
L'Assomption-public building, $24,000.
This is a public building already under contract.

Item agreed to.
Lennoxville-public building, $25,000.
Is this just for a post office or a combination building for postal, customs and other services?
It is a post office on the government-owned site on the corner of Main and Belvedere streets. The postal revenues amount to $11,000.

Item agreed to.
Louiseville-public building-addition, alterations and improvements, $10,000.
This is to provide for an addition to the public building, for increased accommodation for the post office.

Item agreed to.
Montreal, Craig street drill hall-improvements and repairs, $75,000.
What are these repairs and improvements?

Last year, under a vote of the National Defence department, repairs were commenced to the front and back walls of the drill hall, just in front of the Champ de Mars, back of the city hall. When they had put the scaffolding around the building and started to make the repairs, the walls were discovered to be in such a condition that there was no use trying to repair them.
I suppose the contractor discovered that.

The condition of the walls was such that they abandoned the idea of repairing them, and the idea now is to reconstruct the front and back walls. Their condition was such that the man who was undertaking the repairs was forbidden to take away the scaffolding for fear the walls would fall.
Had not a report of the department been prepared on which the tender was let? Was not the condition of the walls known before the letting of the tender?

They could not ascertain the real condition of the walls until after they had started the minor repairs they intended to make. The repair work was undertaken by the National Defence department last year, and the scaffolding is still around the building.

Item agreed to.
Montreal-old examining warehouse-improvements, alterations and repairs, $25,000.

This amount of $25,000 is to provide for alterations and improvements to the third floor of the old examining warehouse, to provide new accommodation for the food and drug laboratory of the Department of Pensions and National Health. The work was requested by the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
That is the place which was abandoned when they moved to new premises?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Montreal - public building - addition and alterations, $10,000.

This amount is required for cleaning the exterior of the old portion of this building, called the first unit, which was built in 1916, to make it harmonize with the new section of the building, called the second unit.
The harmonizing of ideas seems to have been one of the major operations of the government recently. Nice work that, their harmonizing of ideas.

Item agreed to.
Mont Joli-public building, $25,000.
This amount of $25,000 is to provide for the purchase of a site and the erection thereon of a public building for postal purposes in the town of Mont Joli, in the constituency of Rimouski.
That is a terminal point on the railway. A very important community!

Item agreed to.
North Hatley-public building, $13,500.
The contract has been awarded to Mr. J. A. Verret, of Sherbrooke, for the sum of $8,348.
Hatley has at least twenty-five residents.
With summer visitors.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
Perce-public building, $15,500.
Has the contract for this building at Perce been awarded? It is a small village. What is the revenue there? I recall that the postal accommodation was in a very small building.
The contract has been awarded to Mr. Laurent Giroux, of St. Casimir, for the sum of $9,408. The population is over 1,500.
I was just wondering why, if the contract is for $9,000, we have a vote of over $15,000. Surely it would not require the difference for the fittings.
It includes fittings and boxes, $2,000; supervision, $750; lighting plant, $1,500; and contingencies, $1,840.

Item agreed to.
Pointe Claire-public building, $25,000.

Has the contract been
awarded at Pointe Claire?

Yes. The contract was
awarded in December 1937-
A kind of Christmas gift.

Item agreed to.
Pointe au Pic-public building, $28,000.

This is a building for
postal and customs purposes, on a site on the public highway purchased in October, 1937.
It is open in the summer time, I suppose.
And in the winter time, too. The customs revenues are over $8,000, and the postal revenue, over $4,000.
It is a summer resort?
Yes.
It takes the money you collect in the summer to keep up the fire in the winter.

Item agreed to.
Quebec-postal terminal building, $300,000.
What progress has been made with this building?
The plans are pretty nearly complete, and we expect to be in a position to call for tenders in not more than a month or five wreeks.
It depends on how thing go down in the convention.

Item agreed to.

Quebec quarantine facilities-improvements,

The amount of $12,000 was
requested by the Deputy Minister of Pensions and National Health for the following improvements to the ' quarantine facilities at Quebec: Savard park hospital, balance due on contract for erection of unit; amount required to provide metal screens on windows; amount required to repair boundary fencing; grading and planting trees; for fixtures such as dish sterilizer and refrigerator and so on.

Item agreed to.
Quebec West-public building, $12,500.
This is a revote?

This is a revote required for the erection of building for post office services on a site on the corner of Fourth avenue and Third street, purchased in February, 1937. The contract is awarded for $7,775.

Item agreed to.
Rigaud-moving public building, $20,000.

This amount is required
for the expense of moving the post office building. The provincial government is building a bridge over the river in the village of Rigaud, and the bridge comes just to the point where the post office was standing.
The province would pay for moving it, would it not?
We pay for moving our post office.
If their bridge takes away your post office, by expropriation, surely you are not going to pay for moving it, are you?
Well, it may not be a sound undertaking, but we have made it.

I understand you did
that prior to the last provincial election.
Oh, it was done last year.
Twenty thousand dollars seems a large sum. for moving a building. Is it a considerable distance?
Why do you not build a new bridge?
The site was given to us by the municipality.

Item agreed to.
Rock Island customs and immigration building-addition to site, $17,000.
This is an historic name.

It is indeed. This is to provide for the purchase of additional land known as the Bouchard property, in connection with the customs and immigration building at Rock Island. This was requested by the Department of National Revenue.
Is there a house there, or are there any buildings on the land?
There is the Bouchard property, the purchase price of which is 813,000; for demolishing the building, and grading and levelling the property, the estimate is $3,800.
What is the size of the property?
The Bouchard property has a frontage of eighty-three feet on Main street by a depth of ninety-four feet.

I would not think the whole town would be worth that much money. How is an amount of $17,000 arrived at for eighty-three feet in a town that size? What is the assessment of that property? The government have a right to expropriate. They do not have to give three or four prices for a piece of property.
They must give the just price.

The officer of the department made the following report on January 22, 1937:
I visited Rock Island and examined the Bouchard property required by the customs to handle the vehicular traffic. This property, owned by Mr. Bouchard, consists of a lot, number eighty, situate on Main street at the junction of the bridge approach. It has a frontage of eighty-three feet on Main street by a depth of ninety-four feet on the approach to the bridge, and has, according to the official book of reference of the village, an area of 9,700 feet. On the land as it stands there is a three-storey building, sixty-one feet by fifty-seven feet. There are three shops on the first floor and four apartments on the second. The third storey is not finished.
Then it is not vacant property?
No.

Item agreed to.
Rosemount-public building, $25,000.

I should like to know why some consideration is not being given to my constituency? I do not want to be unfair,
but I submit that something should be done there.
When we come to Nova Scotia the hon. gentleman can bring up the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but he is out of order. We are discussing public buildings in the province of Quebec.

Item agreed to.
St. George de Beauce-public building, $29,000. Mr. CARDIN: The population is 1,500, and the revenue, over $8,000.
Item agreed to.
St. Pacome-public building, $12,500.
This is a new building. The population is over 1,200, and the postal revenue, $2,000.

Item agreed to.
St. Raymond-public building, $15,000.
The population is 1,800, and the postal revenue, over $4,000.

Item agreed to.
St. Scliolastique-public building, $18,000.
This is a new building. What is the justification?
The population is over 1,300, and the postal revenue, $2,200.

Item agreed to.
Scotstown-public building, $23,000.

This is a revote, which
indicates that the work has been undertaken. There has been a prior vote. As we have gone through these estimates what strikes one is the large number of revotes. What is the total amount expended last year out of the estimates? It seems to me there must be a very large discrepancy or margin between the votes of last year and the amount actually expended, because we have so many of these revotes. We have the figures of the total estimates, main, supplementary and others for each year; but I should like to know, if it is not too much trouble, the total amount expended out of the estimates last year to the end of the fiscal year?
I can supply that information the next time.

Item agreed to.
Thetford Mines-public building, $60,000.
This is a large sum.

It is an important place. That is the asbestos town.

Sup-ply-Public Works-Buildings
They are all important.
The population of the town is 11,000; postal revenues were $20,000, and customs revenues, $52,000.
What will be housed in this building?
Post office and customs, and they are also providing accommodation for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Will this save rentals of buildings now used for these purposes?
A public building was built there in 1903, a one-storey brick structure. We are tearing it down and building a new one on that site.

Item agreed to.
Thurso-public building, $15,000.

The population there is nearly 1,300, and the postal revenues, $3,400. A fire occurred a short time ago which totally destroyed the building, and the post office has been moved temporarily to another site. That is the information from the Post Office Department.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, June 8, 1938
